CHSA · Aug 7–15, 2026

Selia Tan Cantonese-language Talk — Registration Analysis

Section oneWho is coming

The age profile is the single most consequential fact in this data. 58.1% of those who gave an age are 70 or older, and 74.3% are 60 or older; under-50s are 14.9%. Everything downstream — venue, seating, hearing accessibility, which channels work — follows from that.

5.7% of registrants preferred not to give an age band.

Years in the US

68.8% are foreign-born with more than a decade here, and 10.6% arrived within the last ten years. One in five was born in the US. The Cantonese-language framing worked exactly as intended: this is a long-settled, largely first-generation Cantonese-speaking audience.

10.2% preferred not to answer.

Section twoWhere they live

78.3% of registrants gave a usable ZIP code; the rest left it blank, which the form allowed. Of those who answered, nearly four in five are in San Francisco proper — but only about a third of those are in the walkable Chinatown core, so half the room is travelling across the city.

San Francisco ZIPs

Nine SF ZIPs drew nobody at all: 94104, 94105, 94111, 94117, 94123, 94129, 94130, 94132 and 94158 — the Financial District towers, the Marina, the Haight, the Presidio and Treasure Island.

Outside San Francisco

Grouped by part of the city

Section threeAncestral hometowns

77.1% of registrants named a usable ancestral place; 17.2% left the field blank and 5.7% wrote "NA" or something unreadable. All shares in this section are out of those who named a place.

The field was free text, answered in simplified characters, traditional characters, pinyin and Cantonese romanisation, so the raw answers consolidate roughly four-to-one into distinct places. The Cantonese spellings — Toisan, Sunwui, Jung san, Poon Woo, Seun Dak — are people writing the place as their family says it rather than as pinyin, and they cluster among older and US-born registrants.

Two answers went all the way down to village level, finer than the form asked for and immediately useful for archival matching.

84.3% of those who answered named a specific county; 15.7% gave only a city or a province, which is why the map marks those in red rather than shading a county.

Grouped by native-place region

Three things worth drawing out. Taishan and Kaiping alone account for 57.0% of those who answered, and the three Sze Yup counties together 64.5% — a classic Sze Yup Chinatown audience. But Enping, the fourth Sze Yup county, was named by nobody, and neither was Heshan: the cluster is tighter than "Sze Yup" implies, really Taishan–Kaiping with a Xinhui tail. And Chaoshan and Hakka origins are nearly absent, at 3.3% combined — a Cantonese-language talk self-selects hard, so reaching those families would take separate outreach in a different dialect, not these same channels.

If the talk touches on diaolou, qiaoxiang architecture or village lineage records, most of this audience has direct personal stakes in it, and the Q&A will likely run toward "do you have anything from my village."

Section fourLunch and volunteering

94.9% said yes to the free lunch, and the yes-rate stays high in every age band — so lunch capacity, not the talk, is the binding constraint on registration. No dietary-restriction question was asked, which is worth adding given how senior the crowd is.

63.7% opted in to hearing more about volunteering with CHSA — an unusually high conversion for an event form, and it holds across every age band rather than concentrating among retirees.

23.6% wrote something in the skills box. Of those, 56.8% named a specific skill, 18.9% expressed interest without specifics, and 24.3% were polite declines. Note that a handful wrote in a skill without ticking the volunteer box — they'd be missed by a checkbox-only filter.

Three write-ins deserve a personal reply rather than a form letter: a former CHSA board member who describes securing a state allocation toward acquiring the Julia Morgan building; a registrant offering a video about his family's immigration, covering his father's Angel Island detention and paper-son history; and a registrant in his twenties combining interviewing, archiving, documentary photography and video editing in one person. One more wants to learn interviewing in order to record his own family's history — a training-workshop demand signal.

Section fiveTiming and channels

Two spikes: opening day took 31.2% of all signups within 24 hours, and a second surge on Aug 13–14 took 35.7% between them. A launch push followed by a successful second wave — the form did not simply decay.

84.1% of rows carry a valid channel code; shares below are out of those.

Grouped by medium

Nearly half this audience came through WeChat groups, and seven in eight came through WeChat, a Chinese-language newspaper, or email. Facebook and Instagram together produced 6.8% — consistent with a crowd that is 74.3% over 60.

Within WeChat, one group did most of the work: "Digital Life" alone delivered 25.8% of all coded registrations, almost all of them on launch day, then went quiet. Sing Tao and the ChAm Pioneer Heritage Committee email list carried the entire back half of the campaign, which is what turned a decaying form into a second wave. The lesson for next time is to stage those two rather than fire everything on day one — and to keep the smaller WeChat groups in the rotation, since they cost nothing to post to.

Caveat: 15.9% of rows carry no usable code, so every share here is approximate. Tightening that one field is the cheapest way to make the next event's attribution trustworthy.
